kp.k: Legal aid develops chatbots to centralize fragmented knowledge
kp.d: Ashley Oborn describes Lone Star Legal Aid's chatbot project as an effort to improve productivity and efficiency by reducing time spent finding information needed for client services. Host Cat Moon places the project in an organization with 11 offices serving 76 counties and over 25,000 cases handled in 2024, supported by LSC Technology Initiative Grant funding. These are project motivations and organizational context, not measured chatbot productivity gains.
qs: Lone Star has 11 offices serving 76 counties. They’ve handled over 25,000 cases in 2024.

So I wanted to figure out a way of centralizing all of that information because another passion of mine in particular is centralizing information and getting rid of all these different fragmented sources to create that efficiency and create that productivity for everybody.

kp.k: Juris curates legal research rather than replacing existing platforms
kp.d: Oborn describes the initial proof-of-concept chatbot, Juris, as tailoring research to staff and their clientele. Its function is to gather secondary sources, pair them with black-letter law available through existing platforms such as Westlaw, and ground source selection in subject-matter expertise.
qs: Juris is a legal research chatbot, and Juris wasn’t created to replace other platforms, but mostly curate the way our staff conducts legal research, curated specifically to them in our clientele.

So gathering up secondary sources and pairing them with black letter law that’s already available on platforms such as Westlaw that we have access to is really the key there, but also verifying those sources and grounding them in subject matter experts expertise and what we really want our advocates to have access to and be referencing time and time again.

kp.k: LSLA Ask consolidates administrative knowledge for staff
kp.d: Oborn describes LSLA Ask as an internal administrative assistant that brings together policies, procedures, forms and recurring cross-departmental answers previously dispersed across drives, emails, PDFs and printed materials. The intended change is easier staff access and explanations in users' own language, illustrated by her difficulty understanding the leave policy.
qs: It’s a way of centralizing all of those resources with all of our internal forms and policies and procedures so that anybody can access that information that works at LSLA, of course, and really get that broken down in their own vernacular.
And then also those cross-departmental FAQs that have the same answer on repeat that you give time and time and time again.

kp.k: NAVI targets public legal information and geographically relevant referrals
kp.d: Oborn identifies NAVI as the only external-facing bot, designed for Texans with civil legal issues. Experts help map legal-issue lifecycles in plain language so users can enter at different stages, find information and receive locally relevant referrals to legal aid, shelters or other social services without knowing legal jargon. She describes sourcing expertise across 99 legal issues; the transcript does not report public-use outcomes.
qs: We also then have NAVI, and NAVI is our only external facing bots, and it is what I like to call a resource hub for information and referrals and resources for civil legal issues for Texans.
So you have all of these legal issues, all 99 of these legal issues, and finding experts for all of that was no small task.
It’s going to bring you to the true source of the resource you want to go to or refer you to the correct legal aid in your area based on the county you’re putting in.

kp.k: Expert-vetted datasets underpin the project's trust strategy
kp.d: Oborn argues that curated inputs should precede technical implementation: legal and administrative experts identify and consolidate vetted information before prompting is added. For the public-facing bot, she reports more preparatory steps and comprehensive issue mapping, while retaining the same expert-led sourcing principle. This is the team's accuracy and trust strategy, not an empirical demonstration that errors have been eliminated.
qs: So one of the things that I knew from the very beginning that we wanted to solve is we wanted to really curate and control the information going into these chatbots so that the information going in wasn’t garbage so that we eliminated how much garbage was going to come out.
make sure it’s that true source of vetted information first before you put any technology to it and then add some prompting techniques after that.
I think that my logic for the external bot definitely had a lot more steps behind it before I could get to this point, but it still is backed by the same thing I just went over.

kp.k: Abstention prompts and citations support human verification
kp.d: Sourav Mohan says the team seeks to constrain models' tendency to answer and agree with users by repeatedly instructing them not to answer when supplied sources are insufficient. Internal bots display chapter, section, page number and source excerpts beneath answers so lawyers can check the underlying material rather than blindly rely on output. He describes safeguards without providing measured error rates or test results.
qs: The main thing to understand about large language models is that it wants to give you an answer no matter what, and a lot of times it wants to agree with you.
If you cannot answer based on the sources that we give it, then don’t answer at all.

The other thing we do for our internal chatbots is we have citation that shows up right under the answer and they can now not only see the chapter, the section, the page number that it comes from, but also an excerpt that shows the actual source that used to answer that particular question.
So the whole point of everything we do is just to constrain the large language model.

kp.k: In-house development depended on skills, sponsorship and extended timelines
kp.d: Oborn says existing Python skills enabled an internal passion project alongside regular analytics work. She attributes organizational acceptance to the Juris proof of concept, positive responses at the Innovations and Technology Conference, and respected internal subject-matter experts. Delivery required additional work hours and a deliberately two-year project after the presentation because participants retained full-time responsibilities; Mohan emphasizes managerial permission and balancing existing duties. Oborn also recommends an extra six months of scheduling allowance.
qs: I knew Soro had a penchant for Python coding. I knew he was particularly skilled in it.

So starting with that proof of concept, starting with Juris, debuting it at ITC, which is the Innovations and Technology Conference for whomever doesn’t know that’s listening in. That was our huge win for us strategically and planning this project and getting our work accepted by leadership within our own organization and for others in that matter.
We made this project a two-year long project after we presented Jiras and that was on purpose. We have full-time jobs and everybody else on this project has full-time jobs.
And then building an extra six months.

kp.k: Internal rollout was imminent rather than an established outcome
kp.d: At the recording, Oborn says the two internal bots would launch to all staff that week, with Mohan's presentation scheduled for the next day. This situates the account as development and rollout experience; the transcript supplies no quantified reductions in research time, administrative workload or unmet legal need.
qs: This week, we are launching our two internal bots with all of our staff. Actually, Sue will be doing that presentation tomorrow.

kp.d: Oborn argues that legal aid must use available technological tools to meet otherwise unmanageable need. She cites a 92% access-to-justice gap and says meeting all eligible clients in LSLA's service area would require 17,000 clients per attorney, referring to work for an upcoming panel without supplying a methodology. Moon separately frames the 92% figure as a failure rate. These claims motivate hoped-for scaling, rather than demonstrate chatbot impact.
qs: A 92% access to justice gap.
For every one LSLA attorney, we would have to serve 17,000 clients for our service area alone. There’s no way we’re going to come close to that without using technology.
the 92% failure rate.

kp.k: Speakers favor human augmentation over replacement
kp.d: Oborn characterizes AI as another technology tool rather than a threat to all jobs. Mohan supports augmentation with his own experience repeatedly correcting wrong model outputs, arguing that word prediction is insufficient for difficult questions or tasks while remaining useful for helping staff serve more people. These are qualified practitioner views about capabilities and future service improvement, not labor-market findings.
qs: AI isn’t scary. It’s not over here to overtake all of everybody’s jobs. It’s a technology tool.
I have corrected so many things that large language model has given me because it’s been wrong a lot of the time.
And so the idea that it can replace a human person in the whole transaction is, I think, a little overblown. Maybe I just don’t know enough.
But at the same time, it can be used to make everyone’s life easier so we can serve more people and improve our service area and stuff.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Oborn describes three purpose-specific chatbots intended to improve legal-aid efficiency and access to information; both interviewees frame AI as assistance rather than replacement for human legal-service work.
pts.d: Ashley Oborn describes Juris as a legal-research tool that curates sources for Lone Star Legal Aid's staff and clientele rather than replacing existing research platforms. LSLA Ask centralizes internal policies, forms, procedures and frequently requested workplace information. NAVI, the only external-facing bot, is intended to provide Texans with plain-language civil legal information, resources and geographically relevant referrals. Oborn argues that technology is necessary to address the scale of unmet need. Sourav Mohan claims that large language models can make work easier and help staff serve more people, but their errors and limitations make claims of complete human replacement overblown. These are descriptions of intended functions and predictions about capacity, not reported measurements of improved service delivery.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists principally of firsthand development experience, expert-informed source preparation, anecdotal feedback and figures illustrating unmet need, rather than measured chatbot outcomes.
pts.d: Oborn grounds the proposed benefits in practical experience centralizing fragmented legal and administrative information, consulting subject-matter experts across 99 legal issues, and receiving positive responses to the proof of concept. She cites a 92% access-to-justice gap and a calculation that each LSLA attorney would need to serve 17,000 eligible clients to meet the service-area need; the transcript does not supply the underlying methodology or sources for these figures. These numbers support her account of the need for technology, not a quantified claim about chatbot effectiveness. Mohan bases his caution about substitution on personally correcting numerous model errors. He describes source citations and excerpts that enable staff to verify answers. No measured time savings, accuracy rates, increases in clients served or reductions in unmet need are reported.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Benefits are prospective at the organization-wide internal launch stage and are conditioned on curated sources, constrained responses, human verification and sufficient implementation time.
pts.d: At the time of the episode, Oborn says the two internal bots are launching to all staff that week; she gives no equivalent launch date for NAVI or deadline for achieving capacity gains. The project was deliberately scheduled over two years after the Juris presentation because contributors also held full-time roles, and Oborn advises allowing another six months. Reliability is presented as dependent on expert-vetted information and prompting that instructs the model not to answer beyond its sources. Internal citations support human verification rather than blind reliance. Mohan qualifies his view of human replacement by reference to his own experience and acknowledges that models remain useful despite limitations.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The intended beneficiaries are legal-aid advocates, administrative staff and Texans seeking civil legal help; development also imposes work on technical staff and subject-matter experts.
pts.d: Juris is intended to help LSLA advocates find and check research tailored to their clients. LSLA Ask serves employees across departments by reducing the need to search scattered repositories or repeatedly seek standard administrative answers. NAVI targets people at different stages of a civil legal problem, including those unfamiliar with legal terminology, and aims to direct them to legal aid, shelters or other local services. Broader capacity gains are intended to benefit eligible clients with unmet civil legal needs, rather than enterprise purchasers of legal services. Oborn also reports additional working hours during development. Neither interviewee predicts a specific reduction in legal-aid staffing; their stated framing preserves human involvement.
